blocks.title: Why Prompt Regression Testing with promptfoo matters here

spans.text: Problem statement: A release changes the refund-policy prompt and must prove old behavior still works. The learner's job is not to memorize Prompt Regression Testing with promptfoo; it is to decide what to build or change, what evidence the system may use, and how to tell whether the change improved known behaviors preserved after prompt edits.

Running case: Promptfoo regression pack with assertions and release gates. We will keep this same case through the lesson so each idea has a job: frame the problem, explain the mechanism, choose a design, test the implementation, and decide what to do next.

Before reading on, predict: if the new prompt passes happy paths but fails refusal and citation cases, where would you look first - the input, the state or data, the model boundary, the validation check, or the release process?
The lesson assumes you can learn the vocabulary, then spends its effort on integration choices, failure signals, and checks that make the idea usable in a real system.

items.text: Product framing: Prompt Regression Testing with promptfoo matters when it changes a user-visible decision, release gate, or operational workflow.
Engineering framing: Prompt Regression Testing with promptfoo matters when it changes data, state, prompts, model behavior, tools, schemas, traces, or runtime constraints.
Validation framing: the lesson is not complete until the team can measure known behaviors preserved after prompt edits on examples that resemble the real workload.

Complete worked artifact

items.text: Release change: a prompt or workflow update makes answers warmer, but the team must prove it did not lose required facts, citations, refusals, or safe tool behavior.

blocks.title: Case study: what changed after the first review

spans.text: The first prototype works on the demo path. Then a reviewer runs the uncomfortable case: the new prompt passes happy paths but fails refusal and citation cases. The output still looks confident, which is exactly why the lesson needs a richer artifact.

The team does not restart from scratch. It adds one missing control to Promptfoo regression pack with assertions and release gates: a stricter input contract, better source metadata, a validation assertion, a human-review edge, a rollback trigger, or an audit log depending on where the failure appeared.

items.text: Decision made: keep the thin slice, but block release until the failure is observable and repeatable.
Evidence added: the artifact now shows the input, intermediate evidence, final output, and pass/fail reason.
Metric promoted: known behaviors preserved after prompt edits becomes part of the release gate instead of a dashboard someone checks later.

spans.text: Case-study takeaway: a useful Prompt Regression Testing with promptfoo design makes the wrong answer inspectable before it reaches users.

spans.text: The failure mode to keep in view is concrete: the new prompt passes happy paths but fails refusal and citation cases. Use it as a diagnostic lens while reading every design choice.

items.text: Golden cases are too easy and miss the failures users actually report.
An assertion checks wording but not the required behavior or source.
The release gate averages away a serious failure in a high-risk slice.
The broad warning sign: known behaviors preserved after prompt edits gets worse even though the final answer or artifact still looks polished.

spans.text: Debugging rule: inspect the earliest place where bad evidence can enter and the latest place where validation should have stopped it.
